draft.title: Credit sales and accounts receivable
card: A credit sale is when a business gives goods to a customer now and the customer agrees to pay later. No cash is received on the day of the sale.
The amount the customer owes is called accounts receivable. It is an asset, because the business expects to receive money from it.
A credit sale still counts as sales revenue on the day it is made. Cash does not rise until the customer pays.
When the customer pays, accounts receivable falls and cash rises by the same amount. The business is not richer, as one asset has been swapped for another.
draft.remember: A credit sale makes an asset, accounts receivable, which turns into cash when the customer pays.

a.q: Harbour Hardware in Geelong sells $800 of tools to a builder on credit. What does the business record straight away?
opts: Accounts receivable of $800, an asset
Accounts payable of $800, a liability
Cash rises by $800 from the sale
Accounts receivable falls by $800
a.why: The builder owes $800, so accounts receivable, an asset, rises by $800. Cash does not rise yet because the builder has not paid. Accounts payable is wrong because it records what the business owes, not what it is owed.
a.clue: Has the builder handed over any money yet?

b.q: Priya's Pantry in Ballarat sold $500 of goods on credit to a café. Two weeks later the café pays the full $500. What happens at that point?
opts: Cash rises by $500 and accounts receivable falls by $500
Cash rises by $500 and total assets rise by $500
Cash rises by $500 and accounts payable falls by $500
Sales revenue rises by a further $500
b.why: The café's payment swaps one asset for another: accounts receivable falls by $500 and cash rises by $500, so total assets stay the same. Total assets do not rise, because the sale was already recorded when the goods were sold on credit.
b.clue: The sale was already counted when the goods left the shop.

b.best: Cash rises by $500 and accounts receivable falls by $500

problems.detail: The why for (a) explains accounts payable ('it records what the business owes'). That term belongs to point 2 and should only be mentioned here, not explained.
